title: Sable and the Bell
premise: Kestrel Vane hosts the midnight shift at a failing community radio station, taking calls from listeners who turn out to have died the previous week — and every call hums the same incomplete song. When photographs from their late grandmother's house begin showing an empty chair that pulls the viewer toward it, Kestrel realizes the song is a summons, and the frost creeping across their studio windows is writing the missing verse. Guided by the dead callers, who remember pieces of Kestrel's own childhood better than Kestrel does, they must learn the song's final verse and sing it alone — refusing to harmonize with the choir in the chair — before the frost completes its pattern on the winter solstice. Kestrel sings the ending off-key, alone, breaking the summons; the chair vanishes from every photograph, but one caller's voice remains on the line, now simply a lonely stranger who remembers being loved.
about_author: Paloma Yarrow is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who swears every strange call in this book is based on a real one. She writes horror about the places where grief and static overlap, and lives somewhere the frost arrives early.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Warm Voices
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On the fifth anniversary of the strange calls, a listener named Marisol phones in — and Kestrel finds her obituary, dated six days ago. Marisol hums a lullaby Kestrel half-remembers from childhood before the line fills with frost-crackle. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing, as Kestrel realizes the dead callers aren't threatening; they miss her.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, alternating with Marisol's calls. Sorting grandma's house for sale, Kestrel finds every photograph now contains an empty wooden chair — and staring at it too long leaves them standing in the middle of grandma's parlor with no memory of crossing the room. A second caller, a man who claims to have been Kestrel's neighbor, warns: the chair is a seat being kept for you. Emotional beat: identity unraveling; the past is being edited.

chapters.title: Three Verses and a Silence
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The callers piece together the lullaby — grandma's song, sung to a child Kestrel can't remember being. Frost writes the first three verses across the studio glass, and the final verse stays blank. When Kestrel hums along with Marisol, they wake in the chair, frost climbing their wrists, and barely tear free as the solstice storm arrives. Emotional beat: terror of belonging to something that erases you.

chapters.title: Sung Alone
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. On the solstice, the chair pulls them fully into grandma's parlor, where the dead wait in a choir, singing the verse the frost has finally written. Kestrel must finish the song without joining the harmony — claiming a self the song insists doesn't exist. They sing it wrong, alone, off-key, and the frost shatters. Resolution: the chair vanishes from every photo; one voice stays on the line, a stranger who remembers being loved. Emotional beat: grief accepted, identity chosen.
